idiom_name: event channel: subscription registry + classifier + dispatch policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the component one channel object with three operations — subscribe(topic or type, handler) returning a subscription handle, publish(event) and unsubscribe(handle). Publish derives the routing key from the event (explicit topic or event type), selects the matching subscriptions through the classifier and dispatches each according to the policy: synchronously in registration order, through a bounded queue, or on a thread pool. Keep the registry inside the channel so publishers never hold subscriber references, define the failure and overflow policy explicitly (isolate subscriber errors, bound the buffer, drop or backpressure), and treat the event as an immutable contract shared by both sides. At part level, prefer an Observable utility over a hand-rolled channel; at module or boundary level, prefer a broker client library over a custom channel implementation.
code_sketch:
channel.subscribe('order-placed', handler)    # returns a subscription handle
...
channel.publish({ type: 'order-placed', payload })  # classifier selects matching subscriptions
# dispatch policy: sync | bounded queue | thread pool, with per-subscriber error isolation
channel.unsubscribe(handle)                     # release subscriber and listener state
pitfalls: Letting the channel grow into a service locator or a process-wide singleton, so real dependencies become invisible.
Dispatching over the live registry while a handler subscribes or unsubscribes: iterate over a snapshot.
Leaving delivery semantics undefined: no buffer bound, no overflow policy and no per-subscriber error isolation.
Never unsubscribing: handlers keep dead objects alive and events keep reaching zombies.
Publishing mutable objects: subscribers can modify shared state, causing non-deterministic cross-subscriber interference.
Using a shared topic namespace without a registry: event names drift, collide and become impossible to govern.

Wrong move: Put every Kafka consumer instance in one consumer group and call each instance an independent subscriber -> each record is assigned to only one member, so the other instances miss it -> instead give each logical subscriber its own group when every group must receive every event.

Wrong move: Treat an Amazon SNS publication as proof that critical work is durably processed -> endpoint delivery and consumer completion are separate concerns -> instead subscribe a durable queue and define acknowledgement, retry and dead-letter handling for the subscriber.

Wrong move: Use pub/sub retention as the authoritative state store -> recovery, compaction and backlog semantics can make correctness and repair opaque -> instead keep durable state in a source of truth and use pub/sub as notification or change distribution.
